newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Trade fears seen limiting Brazil rate cuts.
newsitem.headline: Trade fears seen limiting Brazil rate cuts.

text.p: Central Bank policy-makers meeting today to set October interest rates will probably opt for a modest decline to avoid accelerating consumer demand and pressuring trade accounts, economists said.

"They will cut the Central Bank Basic Interest Rate (TBC) to about 1.85 percent in October (from 1.88 percent in September)," said Nilson Teixeira, chief economist for the Rio de Janeiro investment bank Fonte Cindam.
"The Central Bank is worried about the trade deficit so it will go slowly and avoid the risk of having to raise rates later on," Teixeira said.

Brazil's Central Bank Monetary Policy Council Committee (Copom) meets late Monday afternoon to set the TBC and the Rate of Assistance of the Central Bank (TBAN), which are used as reference rates for the Central Bank's rediscount lines.
The bank wants the TBC and the TBAN to serve as the floor and the ceiling, respectively, for Brazil's SELIC market interest rate, which is currently at 1.91 percent.
It will be the first time the Central Bank sets the TBAN rate, so economists were reluctant to sepculate about the spread between the TBAN and the TBC.

But most economists said the Central Bank's decision on the TBC would likely disappoint the market, which expects a steep cut because of recent low inflation figures and a promising inflation outlook.

"The market is looking at a sharp cut in the TBC to about 1.82 percent because inflation has been low and it should remain at about 0.50 percent a month through December," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at BMC bank in Sao Paulo.

Allain said, however, that the Central Bank is worried that a rate cut similar to market expectations might reduce the attractiveness of government securities in Brazil and slow the flow of dollars too much.
"This imposes its own floor of about 1.84 percent a month for the TBC. I don't think the Central Bank could go much lower than that," Allain said.
Most economists predict the Central Bank's interest rate policy will remain cautious throughout the rest of the year.
A Reuter survey Monday of eight brokerages and research firms forecasts an average monthly market interest rate of 1.80 percent by the end of the year, compared to 1.91 percent today.
